t.1.45.1: Śaunaka said: What King Janamejaya then asked his ministers about his father's going to heaven, tell that to me again in full detail.
t.1.45.2: Listen, O brahmin, to how the ministers of the king, when questioned then, all recounted that death of Parikṣit.
t.1.45.3: But you, sirs, know how my father conducted himself, and how that greatly renowned one met his death when his time came.
t.1.45.4: For having heard from you the whole account of my father's conduct, I shall undertake what is good, and never anything contrary to it.
t.1.45.5: Then the ministers, wise and knowing all dharma, being questioned by that great-souled one, spoke these words to King Janamejaya.
t.1.45.6: Your father was righteous and great-souled, a protector of his subjects. Hear how that great-souled one conducted himself here.
t.1.45.7: Having established the four varṇas each in its own dharma, that king, knower of dharma, protected them in accordance with dharma, like Dharma itself in bodily form.
t.1.45.8: The glorious one, of matchless valor, protected the goddess Earth; he had no enemies at all, nor did he hate anyone. Impartial toward all beings, he was like Prajāpati.
t.1.45.10: He supported widows, the helpless, the wretched, and the infirm; pleasing to behold for all beings, he was like a second Soma.
t.1.45.9: Brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras alike remained content in their own duties, O king, well governed by that king.
t.1.45.11: That king, glorious, truthful in speech and firm in valour, whose people were contented and well-nourished, became in the science of archery a pupil of Śāradvata.
t.1.45.12: Your father, O Janamejaya, was dear to Govinda, and that man of great fame was dear to the whole world as well.
t.1.45.13: When the Kurus had dwindled away, the mighty son of Saubhadra was born of Uttarā; because of that he became Parikṣit.
t.1.45.14: The king was skilled in the purpose of a king's dharma and endowed with all virtues; he had conquered his senses, was self-possessed and wise, and was devoted to the service of the elders.
t.1.45.16: Then you, best of men, rightfully obtained this kingdom that has come down through the line of the Kurus, to hold for a thousand years. Though only a child, you were born noble, the protector of all beings.
t.1.45.15: Knowing the six measures of statecraft, of great intellect, supreme in his knowledge of policy and dharma, your father protected these subjects for sixty years. Then he met his destined end, which could not be escaped, at the hands of a serpent.
t.1.45.17: Never has there been a king in this lineage who did not work for the welfare of his subjects and was not dear to them, especially when one beholds the great conduct of the grandfathers, who were wholly devoted to right conduct.
t.1.45.18: How did my father, such a man as he was, meet his death? Tell me exactly; I wish to hear it truly.
t.1.45.19: The Sūta said: Thus urged by the king, all those ministers, devoted to what was pleasing and beneficial to the king, told the lord of men exactly what had happened.
t.1.45.20: Your father, O king, was ever devoted to the hunt, just like the illustrious Pāṇḍu, the foremost of bowmen in battle, having entrusted all the affairs of the kingdom entirely to us.
t.1.45.21: Once, while roaming the forest, he pierced a deer with a feathered arrow, and having wounded it, he swiftly followed that deer into the dense forest.
t.1.45.22: On foot, with his sword girded on and carrying his bow and quiver of arrows, your father could not find the lost deer in the dense forest.
t.1.45.23: Exhausted, advanced in years, sixty years old and burdened by age, and hungry, he saw a sage close by in the great forest.
t.1.45.25: Then the king, afflicted by hunger and fatigue, at once fell under the sway of anger toward that sage, who stood like a post, calm and keeping his vow of silence.
t.1.45.24: That lord of kings questioned the sage, who was observing a vow of silence, but the sage said nothing at all to him, even though he kept on asking.
t.1.45.26: For the king did not recognize that sage, who was keeping a vow of silence; your father, overcome with anger, insulted him.
t.1.45.27: Lifting a dead snake from the surface of the ground with the tip of his bow, he placed it on the shoulder of that pure-souled one, O best of the Bharatas.
t.1.45.28: And the wise one said nothing to him, neither good nor bad; he simply stood just as he was, without anger, bearing the serpent upon his shoulder.
